text: tried to flex the fingers of that hand, they moved. Sluggishly. Imperfectly. He opened his eyes, squinting against the sterile overhead lighting. It buzzed like a swarm of hornets, fluorescent and cold, washing his vision in pale flicker. Movement tugged at his peripheral. Something dark and crumpled near his arm. He forced his head to turn and found a dark scrap of cloth tied around the wrist — blood-black, soaked through, improvised. Tight. Too tight. For one sharp, irrational second, panic surged — restraint, tightness, pressure around the injury— —but as he grabbed at it to pull it away, his fingers sunk into softness where there was once solid resistance. There was skin beneath the cloth. Not metal. No embedded teeth biting into bone. No hum crawling under the nerves. The cuff was gone. His breath hitched. He stared at the soaked bandana like it might vanish if he blinked. He didn’t know how long he stayed there — only that the thought of moving felt like digging through tar. Somewhere, logic tried to wake up: the survivors, the fight, the knife — hands, entirely too many hands, holding him down while something gave way. They helped him. Why? His thoughts slipped sideways again, fragments scattering before he could catch them, too many systems failing to stay upright at once. He let himself fall with them. The tile was cool. Unmoving. Safe enough. Maybe he’d feel less like scorched earth tomorrow. He closed his eyes as exhaustion sept back in, his body sinking under its own weight. For the first time in weeks, the silence didn’t hurt. As he let rest take his mind from the pain, something stirred gently beneath the skin — faint, sluggish, but there. A pulse. A twitch of black beneath the veins. Uroboros. Healing slower than it ever had, but healing all the same. The footage looped. Frame by frame: a blur of limbs, a flash of steel, the cuff’s detonation flaring across the screen with enough discharged energy to reduce the footage to static for a time. Then the aftermath — Wesker down, the survivors scattering like startled birds. On the desk, the cuff’s remains laid in a mangled heap: metal blackened, circuits cracked, the faint stink of burnt insulation still clinging to it. Useless now. Months of sample collecting. Calibration. Research. Resources spent and prototypes lost. Countless trials. All of it — undone. Ruined by four bleeding nobodies with just enough luck to get in his way. Wesker would be out of commission for days, minimum. And he would never be that easy to corner again. That experiment, for all intents and purposes, was over. Herman closed the connection to the RPD feed with an annoyed huff. There was no reason to watch his failed toy twitch on the ground. He leaned back in the office chair, watching the playback one last time, replaying the moment it all began to fail. The survivors closing in. The pile-on. The knife. The break. He dragged his eyes from the video to the telemetry panel. The cuff’s data stream in the final seconds: readouts spiked red across every channel — neural lock, cardiac suppression, total motor collapse. An overload so complete it nearly killed a demigod. For a heartbeat, even the Entity’s signal drops. Herman exhaled a laugh. “Magnificent.” His eyes flicked back to the footage just in time to catch the cuff’s final arc — when the discharged current jumped to the survivor who removed it, the recoil throwing him back. Herman pauses the frame. Studies it. Conductive discharge. Precision voltage. Adaptive response. Interesting. Yes... there’s something there. Herman's gaze lowered to his own arms, tracing the familiar lines of embedded wire diving in and out of the skin. If he could replicate that — fine-tune it, refine it — If he could isolate that charge — not random, not chaotic — but directed, refined— His mori could become something more. Not just efficient. Not merely brutal. Art. He straightens slowly, pulling up the telemetry logs, eyes hungry as he scrolls. The cuff was made for one body. Too specific. Too delicate. The average human body is messier. Variable. It would need to be consistent. Measured. Flexible within a narrow range. Calibrated to multiple subjects. A proper formula. A real challenge to get just right. Which meant he would need test subjects. A pity about Wesker — but failures only prove the system works, even if for a time. Fortunately, survivors were much easier to collect than killers. And it had been so very long since he had truly challenged himself. The Entity hadn’t stopped him before. And that, at least to him, was permission enough. He closed the failed file marked 06-W. Opened a new one. EXPERIMENT 07 – Electrophysiological Adaptation Trials. His pen scratched across the page. A note. A hum. A smile that didn’t reach his eyes. The lights flickered — patient, waiting. “Let’s begin again.”
